messages.say:
This is a Schumacher Electric manual 12V battery charger, likely an older SE-series unit with selectable 2A slow charge and 10A fast charge modes.


A few observations from the photo:


The selector switch is currently set to 2A (slow charge).

The mode switch appears to be in automatic mode.

The analog meter needle is near the high-charge/current side, which usually means the battery is actively accepting charge.

The green “full charge” light does not appear illuminated brightly enough to indicate completion yet, though sunlight makes it hard to tell definitively.


A few practical points about this style of charger:


2A mode is preferable for lawn tractor batteries. It is gentler and reduces overheating/boiling risk.

A typical riding mower battery around 18–35 Ah may take:
~8–20 hours on 2A depending on discharge state.

If the battery was deeply discharged below ~10V, some old automatic chargers may fail to detect it correctly.


Given the mower in the background appears to be a John Deere lawn tractor:


If the battery repeatedly dies after charging, the common causes are:
Battery sulfation/age

Failed voltage regulator

Parasitic drain

Corroded terminals or bad ground


You can verify charging state more reliably with a multimeter:


Resting fully charged battery:
~12.6–12.8V

Engine running:
~13.5–14.5V indicates charging system working.


One thing to be cautious about: older Schumacher chargers like this are not “smart maintainers” in the modern sense. Leaving them connected indefinitely can overcharge a small mower battery. Once fully charged, disconnect it rather than leaving it on for days.

For a typical riding mower battery, 10A is fairly aggressive. It will charge faster, but it is easier to overheat or gas the battery if left too long.


Approximate times:

Battery condition
Estimated time at 10A
Slightly low
30–60 min
Mostly discharged
1–2 hr
Completely dead
2–4 hr

But those are rough estimates because the actual current tapers as voltage rises.


For a small lawn tractor battery, I would not leave a 10A manual charger unattended for hours. Check periodically for:


Battery getting hot

Strong sulfur/rotten egg smell

Excess bubbling


A safer practical approach:


Use 10A for ~30–60 minutes to bring voltage up quickly.

Then switch to 2A to finish charging.


If you want a more precise estimate, the battery label usually lists amp-hours (Ah) or reserve capacity.

This second photo confirms the charger is now set to:


10A

Automatic mode


That is the correct configuration if you want a quicker recovery charge.


The meter needle is still fairly far left, which on these Schumacher meters usually means the charger is still pushing substantial current into the battery — i.e. the battery is not full yet.


For a mower battery in this state, I would estimate:


~1 hour: probably enough to start the mower

~2–3 hours: likely near full charge


I would not leave a small lawn tractor battery on 10A much beyond about 3 hours unless you are monitoring temperature.


A good practical endpoint:


When the needle drops much closer toward the low-current side and stabilizes there, the battery is approaching full.

Then either:
disconnect it, or

switch back to 2A for a gentler finish.


Also, if after charging the mower still only clicks or cranks weakly, the battery itself may be sulfated rather than merely discharged.

The selector is physically slid toward the 10A side in the photo. The labeling is a little confusing because the arrows are offset, but the switch position itself is what matters here.


So unless the photo angle is misleading, it appears to be on 10A fast charge, not 2A.


You can verify another way:


On 2A, these chargers usually barely hum and the meter moves modestly.

On 10A, the transformer hum is more noticeable and the meter tends to sit farther left/high-current while charging a low battery.


If you intended 2A, slide the right-hand switch fully toward the side marked by the red triangle under “2A.”

Yes — this close-up makes it clear. The switch is set to 2A slow charge.


The earlier wider photo was ambiguous because of the angle and the offset arrows. The actual slider position here is aligned with the 2A side.


At 2A:


Expect roughly 8–15 hours for a substantially discharged mower battery.

You can usually get enough charge to start the mower in:
2–5 hours, depending how dead it was.


2A is the better setting for a small lawn tractor battery anyway. Less heat, less stress, lower risk of overcharging.
Can I start mower while connected

You can, but I would not recommend it with that charger connected.


That Schumacher SE-520MA is a basic charger, not a dedicated jump starter or engine-start unit. When the mower starter engages, current demand spikes far beyond what the charger is designed to supply. Possible outcomes:


Charger fuse trips

Charger overheats

Voltage spike damages charger

Nothing bad happens and it starts anyway


The safer sequence is:


Turn charger off / unplug it.

Remove at least one clamp (preferably negative/black).

Start mower normally.

If it starts weakly, reconnect charger afterward.


If you absolutely must try starting while connected:


Keep charger in 10A, not 2A

Do not crank for long

Stop immediately if charger hum changes dramatically or gets hot


But again, this model is primarily a charger, not a boost pack. Disconnecting first is the conservative approach.

This photo shows the left selector is set to automatic, which is the correct choice for a normal mower battery.


Also, the meter position is useful now:


The needle is around the 90–100% region

That suggests the battery is getting close to charged, at least according to this charger’s crude analog meter.


At this point, if it has been charging for a while already, you can probably:


Unplug charger from wall

Remove negative clamp

Remove positive clamp

Try starting mower


I would expect a reasonable chance it starts now unless:


the battery is old/sulfated, or

there is another issue (starter solenoid, bad connection, charging system, etc.).


One caveat: these old Schumacher meters are not precision instruments. A battery can show “charged” yet still collapse under starter load if one cell is weak. So the real test is cranking performance.
